coach_says: You're a piece down, and your only real asset is the two rooks doubled against g2. Rxg2+ cashes them in now: after Qxg2 Rxg2+ Kxg2 Qg6+ you have queen against rooks and bishop, White's king is wide open and the d3 pawn falls, with real chances to save the game. Qe6 is too slow: White plays g3, the g-file goes quiet and the extra piece decides. When you're behind, strike while your pieces are active, before the opponent plugs the hole.

Kh1 steps off the g1-a7 diagonal so ...c4 can't come with discovered check, but it does nothing about your e4 pawn. Only the f6 knight hits it and nothing defends it, so Black just takes it with Nxe4. Before a prevention move, check what's loose: d3 guards e4, opens your c1 bishop, and you can still play Kh1 later if you need it.
also: develop with a useful pawn move

coach_says: After 1.d4 e5 Black is offering a pawn, and the best answer is simply to take it with dxe5. Then Black has to work to get it back. With 2.Nf3 you hand Black a free choice: ...e4 kicks your knight away and gains space, or ...exd4 swaps off the pawn. Against an early gambit, grab the pawn when it's safe and make them prove the compensation.

Black's king is sitting on e7, on the open e-file, right behind your Ne4. Rfe1 lines a rook up on it, so the knight can jump away with discovered check, for example Ng3+ and then Nxf5 wins the bishop. Black has to spend time moving the king. Bd3 lets Black play Ne5, hitting your bishop, and then swap off your strong knight with Bxe4. When the enemy king is on an open file, get a rook onto that file.

Bc8 takes your bishop back home and just loses time, while your king is still stuck in the middle. Nothing forced it: the c6 knight was well defended. Ne5 was the active move: it hits the f3 queen, gains a tempo, and lets you trade off White's powerful d5 bishop with Bxd5. When the position is quiet, look for a move that develops with a threat, not one that undevelops.

Rxa8 is the best move here. You win back material by taking the rook and the position is as good as it can be after the earlier losses. Keep looking for captures that win back what you gave away, like this one.

Castling is as good as anything here: your king gets safe and the rook comes towards the e-file, where Black's queen is sitting. d4 and Nc3 are just as good. Keep developing with gain of time against that queen.

Your f5 bishop was attacked by the e3 knight and moving it back is fine. Bd7 or Be6 were a touch more active, but you're the exchange up and the plan stays the same: develop, keep the king safe, and trade pieces towards an easy endgame.

Kf8 gets your king off the checking file and is perfectly good. Re6, challenging the e-file, was a little more precise, but you're two pawns up either way. Keep trading pieces, especially rooks, to make the extra material count.

Re1 sets a trap: Black's queen on e4 is lined up with the king on e8, so moving your bishop off e2 would win the queen. But Black just castles, which they wanted to do anyway, and the threat is gone. Nc3 is better: it develops a piece and hits the queen at the same time, so Black loses another tempo. Against an early queen, develop with tempo rather than set one-move traps that are easy to dodge.
concept: develop with tempo on the queen

coach_says: Your e6 pawn has no defender and the d4 knight is staring at it. Nxe6 was already a threat, hitting your queen and the f8 rook. Rad8 makes it worse: now Nxe6 forks queen, d8 rook and f8 rook, and you lose material. Before a developing move, check what the enemy knight is attacking: Qb6 or Rae8 guarded e6.

b5 chases the bishop, but it goes to d5 with a double attack: it hits your a8 rook, and the d4 bishop is still hitting g7. After Bd5 Bxd4 Qxd4, White's queen attacks g7 and the h8 rook while the bishop attacks a8, and you can't cover both. Before kicking a piece, look at where it lands. Bxd4 first, trading off the bishop aimed at g7, or Nf6 to develop, kept you fine.
also: double attack on a8 and g7

coach_says: Your knight on g4 and bishop on c5 are already aimed at White's king, and Qh6 brings the queen into the attack: it hits the h4 bishop, which nothing defends, and lines up on the h-file behind it. After Bg3, ...f5 and ...f4 trap that bishop. Be6 guards d5 sensibly but gives White time for b4 and Nc3. When your pieces are gathering around the king, look for a queen move that joins them with a threat.
concept: queen swing hitting loose h4 bishop

coach_says: Black's last move left e6 undefended, and Nxe6 forks the queen on c5 and both rooks on d8 and f8. After Rxd1 Nxc5 Rxf1+ Rxf1 you come out a clean pawn up with the better endgame, and Nxb7 picks up more. c3 is a quiet move that lets the chance go. Every time the opponent moves, ask what they left undefended and whether a knight can hit two things at once.

Recapture with the pawn: cxd5 gets rid of your doubled c-pawns and gives you a strong d5-e5 centre. Nxd5 hits White's queen, but the queen escapes by taking the e5 pawn, which then also attacks your d5 knight and the h5 bishop that nothing defends. You end up a pawn down with loose pieces. When you choose how to recapture, check what the attacked piece can grab on its way out.
also: loose e5 pawn and h5 bishop

coach_says: The c3 pawn was one of the two guards of d4. c4 takes it away, so only the f3 knight is left defending d4, and Black's g-pawn is ready to kick it with ...g4. After that d4 falls. When the opponent's pawns are rolling towards your pieces, don't pull pawns away from the squares those pieces defend. Bb5, pinning the c6 knight and preparing Ne5, kept your centre secure.
concept: c4 left d4 short of defenders

coach_says: Your e4 pawn is passed, and e3 pushes it with a threat on the f2 rook, so White has no time to stop it. Next the pawn heads for e2 while the bishop and queen back it up. Qd5 is a decent square, but it gives White time for Qd2 and Qe3, putting the queen right in front of your pawn to blockade it. Push a passed pawn while it gains tempo, before the opponent can put a piece in front of it.
concept: push the passed pawn with tempo

coach_says: Kb5 walks into a pawn fork: Rxd5+ Rxd5 c4+ hits your king and rook together, and after cxd5 the king and pawn ending is lost because White's king eats your a-pawn. In rook endings, before you move the king, check which squares enemy pawns can attack with check after a trade. Rf6 or Kc5 kept you in the game.

Your e4 pawn is attacked by the f6 knight and the e8 rook, and only the c3 knight guards it. Rfe1 adds a defender, but the knight can be chased with ...b4, and then rooks get swapped off the e-file. f3 guards e4 with a pawn, which can't be chased away, and frees your pieces to go after Black's weak pawns. A pawn up, defend your pawns with pawns when you can and keep the rooks for active jobs.
concept: defend with a pawn, not pieces

coach_says: h3 is fine: it gives your king air and asks the f5 bishop what it wants to do. Bxc6 was a touch sharper, but the difference is tiny. Keep finishing development and look for central breaks like d4 or Ne5.
